name: BMI
description: Computes Body Mass Index as weight÷(height in metres)², dividing weight in kg by height squared. Height is entered in cm and converted internally by dividing by 100.
notes: Enter height in cm (the formula divides by 100 to get metres). BMI is a population screening tool and does not distinguish muscle from fat.

name: Max heart rate
description: Estimates the maximum heart rate in beats per minute using the common formula 220−age. It gives an age-based ceiling used to set exercise intensity zones.
notes: This is a rough population estimate that can be off by 10-20 bpm for an individual. For precise limits, an exercise stress test is needed.

name: Ideal weight (BMI 22)
description: Computes the body weight corresponding to a BMI of 22 for a given height, using 22×(height in metres)². Height in cm is converted to metres by dividing by 100.
notes: Enter height in cm. BMI 22 is a common midpoint of the healthy range; the ideal figure is a guideline, not a strict target.

name: Daily calories
description: Estimates total daily energy expenditure by multiplying basal metabolic rate (bmr) by an activity factor. The result is the calories needed to maintain weight, in kcal per day.
notes: The activity factor typically ranges from about 1.2 (sedentary) to 1.9 (very active); the default 1.5 is moderate. Requires a BMR value as input.

name: Body surface area (Mosteller)
description: Estimates total body surface area with the Mosteller formula, as the square root of height in centimeters times weight in kilograms divided by 3600. It is widely used for drug dosing and physiological normalization.
notes: Height must be in centimeters and weight in kilograms, giving area in square meters. It is an empirical estimate that does not account for body composition or shape.

name: BMR (Mifflin, female)
description: Estimates the daily basal metabolic rate for women using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation from weight, height, and age. It gives the calories the body burns at complete rest to maintain basic functions.
notes: Weight in kg, height in cm, age in years; the −161 constant is specific to females. Multiply by an activity factor to estimate total daily energy expenditure.

name: BMR (Harris-Benedict, male)
description: Estimates the daily basal metabolic rate for men using the original Harris-Benedict equation from weight, height, and age. It represents the resting energy needed to sustain vital functions.
notes: Weight in kg, height in cm, age in years. This is the classic 1919 formula, which tends to run slightly higher than the newer Mifflin-St Jeor equation.

name: BMR (Harris-Benedict, female)
description: Estimates the daily basal metabolic rate for women using the original Harris-Benedict equation from weight, height, and age. It gives the calories burned at rest to maintain basic bodily functions.
notes: Weight in kg, height in cm, age in years; the coefficients are specific to females. As the 1919 formula it typically reads a bit higher than Mifflin-St Jeor.

name: Max heart rate (Tanaka)
description: Estimates maximum heart rate from age with the Tanaka formula, 208 minus 0.7 times age. It is considered more accurate across a wide age range than the older 220-minus-age rule.
notes: Age is in years and the result is a population average in beats per minute; individual maxima can vary by roughly ±10 bpm. It is an estimate, not a substitute for a measured stress test.

name: Target heart rate (Karvonen)
description: Computes a training target heart rate by the Karvonen method, taking the heart-rate reserve (max minus resting) times the desired intensity and adding the resting rate back. It personalizes target zones using resting heart rate.
notes: Intensity is a fraction between 0 and 1 (e.g. 0.7 for 70%), not a percentage. Accuracy depends on correct maximum and resting heart rate values.

name: VO2max estimate (heart rate)
description: Estimates maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) from the ratio of maximum to resting heart rate, scaled by 15.3. A lower resting heart rate relative to maximum indicates greater aerobic fitness.
notes: Result is in mL/kg/min and is a rough estimate; it needs accurate max and resting heart rates. Direct or field-test measurements are more reliable than this heart-rate ratio method.

name: VO2max (Cooper test)
description: Estimates maximal oxygen uptake from the distance run in 12 minutes using the Cooper test formula, (distance − 504.9)/44.73. Greater distance covered corresponds to higher aerobic capacity.
notes: Distance must be in meters run in exactly 12 minutes at maximal effort. The result in mL/kg/min is an estimate that assumes an all-out, evenly paced run.

name: Running pace
description: Computes running pace as time divided by distance, giving the minutes needed to cover each kilometer. A smaller value means a faster pace.
notes: With time in minutes and distance in kilometers, the result is minutes per kilometer. This is the inverse of speed, so lower is faster, not slower.

name: Calories burned (MET)
description: Estimates energy expended during activity as the MET value times body weight in kilograms times duration in hours. Higher-intensity activities have larger MET values and burn more calories.
notes: This form uses the approximation that 1 MET ≈ 1 kcal per kg per hour. Weight is in kg and time in hours; MET values are tabulated per activity.

name: Daily water intake
description: Estimates a daily fluid intake target as body weight in kilograms times 35, giving milliliters per day. It follows the common guideline of about 35 mL of water per kilogram of body weight.
notes: This is a general rule of thumb; actual needs vary with climate, activity, and health, and food provides some water too. Weight in kg gives the result in milliliters.

name: Ideal weight (Devine, male)
description: Estimates ideal body weight for men with the Devine formula, 50 kg plus 2.3 kg for each inch of height over 5 feet. It is used mainly for clinical drug dosing rather than as a fitness ideal.
notes: Height must be entered in inches; only inches above 60 (5 feet) add weight. It is a dosing heuristic, not a health or aesthetic target, and ignores build and body composition.

name: One-rep max (Epley)
description: Estimates the one-repetition maximum (the heaviest liftable once) using the Epley formula, weight times (1 + reps/30). It converts a submaximal set into a projected single-rep strength value.
notes: Most accurate for a moderate number of reps (roughly under 10); accuracy falls off at very high rep counts. Weight can be in any unit and the result matches that unit.

name: Calories from macronutrients
description: Computes total food energy from macronutrient grams using the Atwater factors: 4 kcal per gram of carbohydrate and protein, and 9 kcal per gram of fat. It gives the calorie content of a food or meal.
notes: Inputs are grams of each macronutrient. Alcohol (about 7 kcal/g) and fiber effects are not included in this simplified form.

name: Waist-to-height ratio
description: Computes the waist-to-height ratio by dividing waist circumference by height. It is a simple indicator of central fat distribution, with values around 0.5 or below generally considered healthier.
notes: Waist and height must be measured in the same unit so the ratio is dimensionless. It is a screening indicator, not a diagnosis, and thresholds vary by population.

name: Weight loss from calorie deficit
description: Estimates body-fat mass lost from a total calorie deficit by dividing it by 7700, the approximate calories stored in one kilogram of body fat. A larger cumulative deficit predicts more weight lost.
notes: The 7700 kcal/kg figure is an approximation, and real loss also includes water and lean tissue changes. Deficit is the cumulative total, not a daily value.

name: Steps to distance
description: Converts a step count into distance walked by multiplying steps by stride length and dividing by 1000 to give kilometers. Longer strides cover more distance per step.
notes: Stride length is in meters per step, so steps times stride gives meters, divided by 1000 for kilometers. Stride varies with height and walking speed.

name: Body Surface Area (Du Bois)
description: Estimates body surface area with the Du Bois formula from weight and height, using their fractional powers. The result in square meters is widely used for drug dosing and physiological indexing.
notes: Weight must be in kilograms and height in centimeters; the constant is calibrated to those units. It is an empirical estimate and may be less accurate at extremes of body size.

name: Body Surface Area (Haycock)
description: Estimates body surface area with the Haycock formula from weight and height raised to fixed powers. It is often preferred for children and infants and gives a result in square meters.
notes: Weight is in kilograms and height in centimeters. As an empirical regression it can differ slightly from Du Bois or Mosteller estimates for the same person.

name: Ideal Body Weight (Devine, Male)
description: Estimates ideal body weight for males by the Devine formula, starting at 50 kg and adding 2.3 kg for each inch of height above 60 inches. It is used mainly for medication dosing.
notes: Height must be in inches; the result is in kilograms. The formula is undefined in a meaningful sense below 60 inches, where it would return values at or below the 50 kg base.

name: Ideal Body Weight (Devine, Female)
description: Estimates ideal body weight for females by the Devine formula, starting at 45.5 kg and adding 2.3 kg for each inch of height above 60 inches. It is commonly used for drug dose calculations.
notes: Height is in inches and the result in kilograms; the base weight is lower than the male version. Below 60 inches it returns values at or under the 45.5 kg base and has limited validity.

name: Lean Body Mass (Boer, Female)
description: Estimates lean body mass in females by the Boer formula from weight and height, using fixed coefficients and a constant offset. It approximates the non-fat mass of the body in kilograms.
notes: Weight in kg and height in cm, matching the calibrated coefficients. It is a population regression and may be inaccurate at obesity extremes or in athletes.

name: Karvonen Target Heart Rate
description: Computes a training target heart rate by the Karvonen method: it takes the heart-rate reserve (maximum minus resting rate), scales it by the desired intensity fraction, and adds back the resting rate. The result is the heart rate to aim for during exercise.
notes: Intensity is a fraction between 0 and 1, not a percentage; 0.7 means 70 percent. Accuracy depends on true resting and maximum rates, which are often estimated.

name: One-Rep Max (Brzycki)
description: Estimates the one-repetition maximum (the greatest weight liftable once) from a weight lifted for several repetitions, using the Brzycki formula. It divides the weight by a factor that shrinks as the repetition count rises, so more reps at a given weight imply a higher one-rep max.
notes: Only valid for roughly 1 to 10 reps; accuracy drops sharply at high rep counts and the formula fails at 37 reps (division by zero). It is an estimate, not a measured max.

name: Power-to-Weight Ratio
description: Divides power output by body weight to give the power-to-weight ratio, a key measure of endurance performance in cycling and running. A higher value means more power available per kilogram of body mass.
notes: Both inputs must be instantaneous or averaged over the same interval. Body weight, not total system weight, is used here; add equipment mass separately if needed.

name: METs Energy Expenditure
description: Estimates calories burned during activity from the metabolic equivalent (MET) value, body weight, and duration. It uses the standard relation that one MET equals 3.5 mL of oxygen per kilogram per minute, converting oxygen use into kilocalories.
notes: Assumes a resting metabolic rate of 3.5 mL/kg/min, which varies between people. Duration is in minutes; result is total kcal for the session, not per minute.

name: Running Calorie Expenditure
description: Estimates the energy used while running from body weight and distance, using the approximation that about 1.036 kcal is burned per kilogram of body weight per kilometer run. It depends on distance rather than speed or time.
notes: Gross (not net of resting metabolism) estimate that ignores pace, terrain, and running economy. Distance is in kilometers; the coefficient bakes in typical running efficiency.

name: Cycling Calorie Expenditure
description: Estimates the calories a cyclist burns from average mechanical power, duration, and muscular efficiency. Mechanical work in kilojoules is divided by efficiency to get metabolic energy, which is then converted to kilocalories.
notes: Efficiency is a fraction (about 0.20 to 0.25 for cycling). The factor 3.6 converts watt-hours to kilojoules and 4.184 converts kilojoules to kilocalories.

name: Projectile Sport Range
description: Calculates the horizontal range of a projectile launched over level ground, from launch speed, launch angle, and gravity. Range is the speed squared times the sine of twice the angle, divided by gravitational acceleration.
notes: Angle must be in radians. Ignores air resistance and assumes equal launch and landing heights, so it overestimates real sporting ranges. Maximum range occurs at 45 degrees.

name: Body Mass Index
description: Computes the body mass index by dividing body weight in kilograms by the square of height in meters. BMI is a simple screening figure used to categorize underweight, normal, overweight, and obese ranges.
notes: Height must be in meters, not centimeters. BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat and can mislead for very muscular or elderly people.

name: Allometric Strength Index
description: Scales total weight lifted by body weight raised to the two-thirds power to give an allometric strength index. This adjustment compares strength fairly across athletes of different body sizes, since strength scales roughly with cross-sectional area.
notes: Dimensionless index for ranking only, not an absolute quantity. Uses the two-thirds exponent from geometric scaling; other standards use different exponents.

name: Body Fat (US Navy, Male)
description: Estimates male body-fat percentage from waist, neck, and height using the US Navy circumference method. The logarithm of waist minus neck and the logarithm of height feed an empirical formula tuned to match hydrostatic weighing.
notes: For males only and uses base-10 logarithms; all lengths in centimeters. It is a statistical estimate that can err by several percent for individuals.

name: BMR (Mifflin-St Jeor, Male)
description: Estimates the basal metabolic rate for males using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, the daily energy the body uses at complete rest. It combines weight, height, and age with fixed coefficients and adds a constant of 5 for males.
notes: Male-specific (the female version subtracts 161 instead of adding 5). Weight in kilograms, height in centimeters, age in years; result is resting energy, before any activity factor.

name: Maximum Heart Rate
description: Estimates the age-predicted maximum heart rate with the classic rule of 220 minus age. It gives an upper bound on heart rate used to set exercise intensity zones.
notes: A rough population average with a standard deviation of about 10 to 12 bpm, so individuals vary widely. Newer formulas like 208 minus 0.7 times age fit data better.

name: Waist-to-Hip Ratio
description: Divides waist circumference by hip circumference to give the waist-to-hip ratio, a standard measure of body fat distribution used to assess health risk.
notes: Measure both circumferences with the same unit and a relaxed, unstretched tape. Higher ratios indicate more abdominal fat and are associated with greater cardiometabolic risk.

name: Calories from macros
description: Estimates total food energy from macronutrients using 4 kcal per gram of carbohydrate, 4 per gram of protein, and 9 per gram of fat.
notes: Uses standard Atwood energy factors; alcohol (about 7 kcal/g) and fiber are not included. Real values vary slightly by food.

name: Body fat mass
description: Estimates the mass of fat in the body by multiplying total body weight by the body-fat percentage. The result is the weight of fat tissue in kilograms, with the remainder being lean mass.
notes: Body fat must be entered as a percent value (20 for 20%), not a fraction. The percentage itself comes from a separate measurement such as calipers or a bioimpedance scale and carries its own error.

name: Lean Body Mass (Boer, Male)
description: Estimates lean body mass for adult males using the Boer formula: 0.407 times weight plus 0.267 times height minus 19.2. It approximates the body mass excluding fat, in kilograms.
notes: This is the male-specific equation; the female version uses different coefficients. Weight must be in kg and height in cm to match the fixed coefficients.

name: Blood Volume (Nadler, Male)
description: Estimates total blood volume for adult males using Nadler's equation, combining a term in height cubed with terms in weight and a constant. The result is total blood volume in liters.
notes: This is the male formula; height is converted from cm to meters (h/100) before cubing, and weight is in kg. The female version uses different coefficients.

name: Basal Metabolic Rate (Mifflin-St Jeor, Male)
description: Estimates basal metabolic rate for adult males using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation: 10 times weight plus 6.25 times height minus 5 times age plus 5. It gives the daily resting energy expenditure in kilocalories.
notes: This is the male form (the female version ends in minus 161). Weight is in kg, height in cm, age in years; multiply by an activity factor for total daily energy needs.

name: VO2max (Rockport Walk Test)
description: Estimates maximal oxygen uptake in mL/kg/min from a 1-mile walk, using body weight (lb), age, sex (1=male, 0=female), the walk time in minutes and the heart rate right at the finish. It gives an aerobic fitness score without a maximal effort test.
notes: Body weight must be in pounds and time in decimal minutes; the sex term adds 6.315 for males. Valid only for a brisk 1-mile walk with heart rate taken immediately on finishing.

name: VO2max (Uth-Sorensen Estimate)
description: Estimates maximal oxygen uptake in mL/kg/min simply from the ratio of maximum to resting heart rate, multiplied by 15.3. Because a lower resting heart rate raises the ratio, fitter individuals get a higher estimate.
notes: Requires an accurately measured resting heart rate and a true maximal heart rate; using an age-predicted HRmax adds error. It is a population estimate, not a lab-grade measurement.

name: ACSM Running VO2
description: Gives the oxygen cost of running in mL/kg/min from the ACSM metabolic equation, adding a horizontal term (0.2 per m/min), a vertical term for grade, and a resting 3.5 baseline. It predicts the aerobic demand of a given speed and incline.
notes: Speed must be in m/min and grade as a decimal fraction (0.02 = 2%), not a percent. Valid for true running (speeds above about 134 m/min), not walking.

name: ACSM Walking VO2
description: Gives the oxygen cost of walking in mL/kg/min from the ACSM equation, with a horizontal term (0.1 per m/min), a larger vertical term for grade (1.8), and the 3.5 resting baseline. It estimates the aerobic demand of walking at a set speed and incline.
notes: Speed must be in m/min and grade as a decimal fraction, not a percent. Valid for walking speeds of roughly 50 to 100 m/min; outside that range it loses accuracy.

name: Cycling Power (Martin Model)
description: Computes the mechanical power in watts a cyclist must produce on flat ground, summing rolling resistance and aerodynamic drag (which grows with speed squared), multiplying by speed, and dividing by drivetrain efficiency. Aerodynamic drag dominates at higher speeds.
notes: This flat-ground form omits any gravity term for slopes and neglects acceleration and wind; speed is ground speed but drag depends on air speed. Efficiency eta is a fraction near 0.97.

name: Cycling Power-to-Weight Ratio
description: Divides power output in watts by body mass in kilograms to give watts per kilogram, a key climbing and endurance metric in cycling. Higher W/kg means a rider can sustain more power relative to the weight they must move uphill.
notes: The comparison is only meaningful with a matched duration (for example 20-minute or 5-second power). Use body mass, or system mass including bike, consistently across riders.

name: Maximum Heart Rate (Tanaka Formula)
description: Estimates age-predicted maximum heart rate in beats per minute as 208 minus 0.7 times age. Derived from a large meta-analysis, it is generally more accurate across ages than the older 220-minus-age rule.
notes: It is a population average with a standard deviation of about 10 bpm, so individual true HRmax can differ substantially. Not a substitute for a measured maximal test.

name: Maximum Heart Rate (Gulati Formula)
description: Estimates maximum heart rate in beats per minute as 206 minus 0.88 times age, a formula derived specifically for women. It typically predicts a lower HRmax than male-based equations at the same age.
notes: Developed and validated in women; applying it to men is inappropriate. Like all age-based formulas it is an average and individual values vary by roughly 10 bpm.

name: Heart Rate Reserve
description: Computes the heart rate reserve in beats per minute as the difference between maximum and resting heart rate. This span represents the usable range of the heart and underlies the Karvonen method for setting training intensities.
notes: Both inputs must be in bpm and the resting value should be a true rest measurement. The reserve itself is not a target heart rate; a percentage of it is added to resting HR for that.

name: Jump Height from Flight Time
description: Estimates vertical jump height in meters from the airborne flight time, as g times time squared divided by 8. It assumes the body leaves and lands at the same height, so the rise time is half the total flight time.
notes: Requires that takeoff and landing occur at identical body positions; bending the knees on landing inflates the result. Flight time must be measured accurately, as height scales with its square.

name: Vertical Jump Height (Takeoff Velocity)
description: Computes the maximum height of a vertical jump in meters from the takeoff velocity, as v squared divided by twice gravity. It converts the upward kinetic energy at takeoff into the peak rise of the center of mass.
notes: Uses the vertical component of takeoff velocity only and ignores air resistance. The result is the rise of the center of mass, not the reach or standing jump-and-reach measurement.

name: Peak Power (Sayers Equation)
description: Estimates peak anaerobic power in watts from a countermovement jump, as 60.7 times jump height in centimeters plus 45.3 times body mass in kilograms minus 2055. It is widely used to gauge lower-body explosive power.
notes: Jump height must be in centimeters and mass in kilograms; mixing units breaks it. It is a regression estimate for countermovement jumps, not a direct force-plate measurement.

name: Projectile Range from Height (Shot Put)
description: Computes the horizontal range in meters of a projectile released from a height above the ground, from its release speed, angle, and height, using the full projectile equation. It accounts for the extra distance gained because landing is below the release point.
notes: Release angle is entered in degrees and converted internally to radians. Air resistance is neglected, so it slightly overestimates real shot-put or throwing distances.

name: Optimal Release Angle (Projectile from Height)
description: Gives the release angle in degrees that maximizes horizontal range when a projectile is launched from a height above the landing point, from the release speed and height. The optimum is always below 45 degrees and decreases as release height rises.
notes: Result is in degrees. It ignores air resistance and biomechanical limits, so real athletes often release slightly lower than this theoretical optimum.

name: Wilks Coefficient (Powerlifting, Men)
description: Computes the men's Wilks coefficient from body weight in kilograms using a fifth-degree polynomial in the denominator. Multiplying a lifted total by this coefficient normalizes strength across body weights so lifters of different sizes can be compared.
notes: Body weight must be in kilograms and this is the male-specific polynomial. It gives the coefficient only; multiply it by the total lifted to obtain the Wilks score.

name: Froude Number (Gait Analysis)
description: Computes the dimensionless Froude number of walking, as speed squared divided by gravity times leg length. It compares inertial to gravitational forces during gait; values near 0.5 mark the typical walk-to-run transition.
notes: The result is dimensionless, so all inputs must be in consistent SI units. Leg length is the pivot-to-ground length; using stature instead changes the value.

name: Batted-Ball Exit Velocity (Restitution)
description: Computes the exit velocity in m/s of a struck ball from the bat and ball masses, their speeds, and the coefficient of restitution, using one-dimensional collision mechanics. It predicts how fast the ball leaves the bat after impact.
notes: Use a sign convention for velocities: an approaching pitch is negative here. The coefficient of restitution between 0 and 1 sets how much relative speed is retained.

name: Riegel Race Time Prediction
description: Predicts a race time from a known performance at another distance, scaling the known time by the distance ratio raised to the 1.06 fatigue exponent. It reflects that pace slows as distance grows.
notes: Distances must share the same unit since only their ratio matters. Best for endurance events over similar terrain; extrapolating far beyond the known distance loses accuracy.

name: Resting Metabolic Rate (Cunningham)
description: Estimates resting metabolic rate in kilocalories per day from lean body mass, as 500 plus 22 times the lean mass in kilograms. Because it uses fat-free mass, it suits lean and athletic populations.
notes: The input is lean body mass in kilograms, not total body weight; using total weight overestimates. Requires a body-composition measurement to obtain lean mass.

name: Basal Metabolic Rate (Katch-McArdle)
description: Estimates basal metabolic rate in kilocalories per day from lean body mass, as 370 plus 21.6 times the lean mass in kilograms. Basing it on fat-free mass makes it accurate across a range of body-fat levels.
notes: The input must be lean body mass in kilograms, not total weight. It gives resting energy only; multiply by an activity factor for total daily expenditure.

name: One-Rep Max (Lombardi)
description: Estimates the one-repetition maximum in kilograms from a submaximal set, as the weight lifted times the repetition count raised to the 0.10 power. More reps at a given weight imply a higher true maximum.
notes: Weight and result share units, so pounds in gives pounds out. Accuracy falls as reps rise beyond about ten; keep the set relatively heavy for a reliable estimate.

name: One-Rep Max (O'Conner)
description: Estimates the one-repetition maximum in kilograms as the weight lifted times one plus 0.025 times the repetition count. Each additional rep adds 2.5 percent to the estimated maximum in this linear model.
notes: Weight in and out share units. The linear form is simple but overestimates the max at high rep counts; it is most reliable for sets under about ten reps.

name: Critical Velocity (Two-Distance Model)
description: Estimates critical velocity in m/s from two maximal efforts, as the difference in distance divided by the difference in time. It approximates the highest speed sustainable without continually drawing down anaerobic reserves.
notes: Both efforts should be all-out and distances in meters with times in seconds. Two points give a rough estimate; more distances and fully exhaustive trials improve reliability.

name: Anaerobic Speed Reserve
description: Computes the anaerobic speed reserve in m/s as the difference between maximal sprint speed and the velocity at VO2max. This band shows how much faster an athlete can go above their aerobic ceiling, informing interval-training design.
notes: Both speeds must be in the same units and measured under comparable conditions. It is a range, not a pace target; athletes with equal VO2max velocity can have very different reserves.

name: Daniels VO2 from Velocity
description: Estimates the oxygen cost of running in mL/kg/min from running velocity using Daniels and Gilbert's quadratic equation. It underlies the VDOT system for prescribing training paces from race performances.
notes: Velocity must be in meters per minute. It models the aerobic demand of steady running and is the running-economy half of the VDOT calculation, not VDOT itself.

name: Cycling Power on a Climb
expression: v * (m * g * (sin(atan(gr)) + crr * cos(atan(gr))) + 0.5 * rho * cda * v^2)
description: Estimates the power a cyclist needs at a steady speed on a gradient: lifting, rolling resistance and air drag.
notes: Add about 2–3 % for drivetrain losses.
